 Jerusalem Post / Business & Innovation / Banking & Finance Your Taxes: ITA extends deadline for aliyah tax break, but it’s not plain sailing
 The aliyah deadline for extra Israeli tax relief on Israeli income has been extended from the end of 2026 to February 10, 2027. This is thanks to the recent election.
 Follow us on Google California’s proposed wealth tax is putting business domicile under scrutiny in exit planning. ( photo credit : SHUTTERSTOCK ) By LEON HARRIS NOVEMBER 20, 2026 21:00 The aliyah deadline for extra Israeli tax relief on Israeli income has been extended from the end of 2026 to February 10, 2027. This is thanks to the recent election.
 But what is this extra tax relief, and aside from arriving in Israel in time, what are the other aliyah tax issues?
 Israel tax breaks in a nutshell 
 Foreign-source income and gains of olim (new immigrants) are exempt from Israeli tax for 10 years – an Israel “tax holiday.” But if olim take up Israeli residence in 2026 onward, they must still disclose (but not pay tax on) exempt income and gains to the Israel Tax Authority (ITA).
 There are special capital-gains tax reliefs if you were away from Israel for only six years and for olim who sell capital assets after the 10-year tax holiday.
 Israel's Tax Authority prepares a NIS 10B reform. (credit: SHUTTERSTOCK) Regarding Israeli-source business or employment income, there is another, more limited, five-year Israeli tax exemption if someone takes up Israeli residence in the period November 5, 2025, to February 10, 2027.
 The limits are NIS 600,000 of income in 2026, NIS 1 million in 2027, NIS 1m. in 2028, NIS 350,000 in 2029, and NIS 150,000 in 2030. Additional conditions apply. There are also certain customs tax breaks and an aliyah cash “basket” payment not discussed here.
 Foreign tax position 
 Always check the foreign tax position and not only Israeli tax breaks. For example, US citizens and Green Card (Permanent Resident Card) holders generally need to keep filing US tax returns, and there are detailed rules for US olim in the Israel-US tax treaty. We sometimes see olim paying tax to the wrong government. Double taxation may then ensue.
 Check all taxes, including capital-gains tax and estate tax or inheritance tax. Check especially the year of transition and visits back to the old country.
 Foreign pensions and retirement payments 
 Once the 10-year tax holiday is over, foreign pensions are usually exempt from foreign tax under Israel’s tax treaties, but they are taxable in Israel. There are two main Israeli tax reliefs: a 35% exemption; and a restriction of Israeli tax to the foreign tax that would apply where the pension is paid.
 The term “pension” is not clearly defined. It may be understood to include lump-sum pension payments and retirement-fund payments, for example, from a US individual retirement account (IRA).
 Foreign business 
 Several issues need checking out if an immigrant has a foreign business or shares in a foreign company.
 First, a foreign company that is controlled and managed from Israel should not be considered Israeli resident and taxable on worldwide income for 10 years.
 Nevertheless, a foreign company may be deemed to have a taxable “permanent establishment” (i.e., a branch) in Israel. The branch may not be taxed in Israel if it stems from an individual who took up Israeli residence in the period November 5, 2025, to February 10, 2027.
 The branch may still be taxed if the individual moved to Israel before or after that period: if there are other employees or shareholders in Israel, or if there is a warehouse or point of sale in Israel, etc.
 Second, commencing in 2025, Israel taxes certain active undistributed “trapped profits” of private closely held companies (five or fewer shareholders). This is done by attributing company profits to the shareholders and taxing them at rates up to 50%.
 It seems this applies to foreign companies of immigrants in Israel unless they are eligible for the abovementioned limited Israeli-source income exemption. Unfortunately, the ITA still has not published guidance in this area.
 Any immigrant with a company or business abroad should check out these issues, as solutions do exist.
 ESOP issues 
 Israel has special rules regarding employee share ownership plans (ESOPs). Typically, an ESOP with an approved Israeli trustee for two years or more may confer deferred and reduced Israeli taxation: 25%-30% tax in applicable cases.
 Two issues often arise. First, a foreign ESOP may not comply with the Israeli ESOP rules. Second, the ITA denies the 10-year aliyah tax holiday to ESOP gains relating to a foreign company, including US big tech group ESOPS. This is highly controversial.
 Inherited foreign assets 
 Israel repealed the inheritance tax in 1981. If you inherit a foreign property or securities portfolio, however, you still pay Israeli capital-gains tax when you sell these assets, even if there was estate or inheritance tax abroad. And your cost is the historic cost of the deceased unless you request a special step-up procedure. Check it out.
 As always, consult experienced professional advisers in each country concerned at an early stage in specific cases.
